faqSection.title: Everything You Need to Know Before Your Visit
faqSection.text: Clear answers to the most common questions from our patients about surgeries, consultations, and medical insurance.

items.q: Is microscopic brain and nerve surgery completely safe?
items.a: Yes, thanks to 3D neuronavigation and real-time neuromonitoring, safety rates are significantly higher and complications are minimized compared to traditional surgery.

items.q: How long is the recovery after endoscopic spine surgery?
items.a: In most cases, patients can walk the same day and return to desk work within one to two weeks, while strenuous physical activity requires 4-6 weeks.

items.q: Is surgery required immediately after a disc herniation diagnosis?
items.a: Not necessarily. We follow a gradual approach starting with conservative treatment and image-guided injections, resorting to surgery only when conservative treatment fails or progressive neurological weakness appears.

items.q: Do you work with health insurance companies?
items.a: Yes, we work with most locally and internationally accredited health insurance providers, and our reception team can help verify your policy coverage before your appointment.

items.q: Can patients outside Egypt get a remote consultation?
items.a: Absolutely. We offer initial video consultations to review scans and medical reports before planning your travel and treatment schedule.

items.q: What documents and tests are needed before the first visit?
items.a: We recommend bringing all previous scans (MRI or CT) along with medical reports and relevant lab results for an accurate assessment during your first consultation.

items.q: What's the difference between open surgery and minimally invasive surgery?
items.a: Minimally invasive surgery relies on very small incisions and precise endoscopes, reducing pain, bleeding, and hospital stay compared to traditional open surgery.

items.q: Do all disc herniation cases require surgery?
items.a: No, most cases respond to conservative treatment and physiotherapy; surgery is reserved for cases with neurological weakness or failed conservative treatment.

items.q: How long does it take to get imaging results and a diagnosis?
items.a: Scans are typically reviewed and an initial diagnosis is made during the same first consultation session.

items.q: Are there safe anesthesia options for elderly patients?
items.a: Yes, every case is assessed by a specialized anesthesia team to select the safest protocol based on age and overall health.

items.q: Can I get a second opinion?
items.a: Absolutely, we welcome reviewing reports and scans of previously diagnosed cases to provide an independent medical opinion.

items.q: What is the post-surgery follow-up process?
items.a: We set a clear schedule for follow-up appointments, checkups, and physiotherapy sessions if needed, to ensure the best possible recovery.

items.q: Is emergency service available around the clock?
items.a: Yes, a hotline for neurological emergencies is available 24/7.

items.q: Can I get a detailed medical report in English?
items.a: Yes, we provide all medical reports and correspondence in both Arabic and English to facilitate communication with insurance companies or overseas treatment centers.

hero.subtitle: Accurate, reliable medical content explaining the latest scientific developments in neurosurgery and spine surgery.

featured.title: The Neuronavigation Revolution: How Technology Transformed the Future of Brain Tumor Surgery
featured.text: An in-depth look at how 3D surgical navigation systems and intraoperative imaging raise safety and precision rates in resecting complex brain tumors, with real case studies from the operating room.
content: Neuronavigation works like a GPS system for the brain. Before surgery, a patient's MRI and CT scans are fused into a detailed 3D map, which the surgical team uses in the operating room to track instruments in real time relative to the tumor and the surrounding healthy tissue.

This precision translates directly into safer outcomes: smaller incisions, more accurate margins around critical areas that control speech, movement, and vision, and a significantly reduced risk of damaging healthy brain tissue during resection.

It is important to understand that navigation technology supports the surgeon's judgment rather than replacing it — it is most powerful when combined with intraoperative imaging and an experienced surgical team. Every case is different, and the right approach is always determined after a thorough evaluation with your neurosurgeon.

items.title: When Should You See a Neurosurgeon Without Delay?
items.text: Critical warning signs such as sudden limb numbness, escalating headaches with blurred vision, or disturbed balance and coordination.
content: Certain neurological symptoms should never be watched and waited on. Sudden numbness or weakness in an arm or leg, a severe headache that keeps getting worse and comes with blurred or double vision, and a sudden loss of balance or coordination are all signs that deserve immediate medical attention.

The reason timing matters so much is that many neurological conditions, from bleeding and clots to tumors and nerve compression, respond far better to treatment when caught early. A delay of even a few hours can change the course of recovery in some cases.

Experiencing one of these symptoms does not automatically mean surgery is needed; many cases are resolved with monitoring or medication. But a prompt evaluation by a neurosurgeon is the only way to know for certain, so don't hesitate to reach out to our clinic or the nearest emergency department.

items.title: What's New in Brain Tumor Treatment: Neuronavigation & Limited Intervention
items.text: How CT imaging and 3D navigation systems during surgery raise safety rates and enable near-complete tumor resection.
content: The treatment of brain tumors has shifted decisively toward minimally invasive approaches. Where once a large craniotomy was the only option, many tumors today can be reached through smaller, precisely planned corridors guided by advanced imaging.

Techniques such as endoscopic tumor removal, intraoperative MRI, and awake craniotomy, where the patient remains conscious so the team can map speech and movement in real time, allow surgeons to remove more of the tumor while protecting critical brain function.

The result for patients is a more personalized treatment plan, shorter hospital stays, and faster return to daily life, with the surgical strategy tailored to the tumor's size, location, and relationship to the surrounding brain structures.

items.title: Effective Ways to Prevent Lower Back Pain for Office Workers
items.text: Simple stretching exercises and evidence-based sitting postures to protect the lumbar and sacral spine from chronic pressure and disc herniation.
content: Long hours seated at a desk put sustained pressure on the discs and muscles of the lower back, especially when posture is poor or the workstation isn't set up correctly. Over time, this can lead to chronic stiffness and pain.

Simple habits make a real difference: keep your screen at eye level, your lower back supported by the chair, and your feet flat on the floor. Stand up and move for a few minutes every 45 to 60 minutes, and build a habit of gentle core and back-strengthening exercises a few times a week.

If the pain becomes persistent, radiates down the leg, or is accompanied by numbness or weakness, it's a sign that self-care alone isn't enough. A spine specialist can identify the underlying cause and recommend the right treatment path.

items.title: Pituitary Tumors: Symptoms You Should Never Ignore
items.text: From chronic headaches to vision and hormonal disturbances, learn the early signs and endoscopic treatment options.
content: The pituitary gland is small, about the size of a pea, but it regulates many of the body's essential hormones. Most pituitary tumors are benign, but because of the gland's location and function, even a small growth can have a noticeable effect.

Warning signs include persistent headaches, changes in peripheral vision, unexplained fatigue, irregular menstrual cycles, or unusual changes in growth or body proportions. These symptoms occur either because the tumor is pressing on nearby structures or because it is disrupting normal hormone levels.

Diagnosis typically involves an MRI scan alongside a hormonal blood panel. Many pituitary tumors today can be removed through the nose using endonasal endoscopic surgery, avoiding open skull surgery entirely and allowing for a considerably faster recovery.

items.title: Cerebral Aneurysms: Can They Be Treated Before They Rupture?
items.text: The importance of early screening for at-risk individuals and modern interventional catheterization treatment options.
content: A cerebral aneurysm is a weak, bulging spot in the wall of a brain blood vessel. Most aneurysms never rupture and cause no symptoms at all, which is why many are discovered incidentally during imaging done for an unrelated reason.

Risk factors for growth and rupture include high blood pressure, smoking, and a family history of aneurysms or connective tissue conditions. When an aneurysm is found early, monitoring or preventive treatment can significantly reduce the risk of a life-threatening rupture.

Two main treatment options exist today: microsurgical clipping, performed through open surgery, and endovascular coiling, a minimally invasive procedure performed through the blood vessels. The right choice depends on the aneurysm's size, shape, and location, and is decided together with your neurosurgeon.

items.title: Refractory Epilepsy: When Is Surgery the Best Option?
items.text: Modern treatment options for drug-resistant epilepsy patients that go beyond traditional medication.
content: Epilepsy is generally considered drug-resistant, or refractory, when seizures continue despite trying at least two appropriately chosen medications at adequate doses. This affects a meaningful share of people living with epilepsy and often significantly impacts quality of life.

The evaluation for surgical candidacy is thorough: it typically includes video-EEG monitoring to record seizures as they happen, along with detailed brain imaging to pinpoint the exact region where the seizures originate.

When a clear, safely operable seizure focus is identified, surgery can be transformative. A large proportion of carefully selected patients become seizure-free or see a dramatic reduction in seizure frequency, often allowing them to reduce their medication burden as well.
